sun.short_description: The Sun is the star at the center of the Solar System and the only object in this catalog observable exclusively with dedicated protections. In white light, a certified solar filter mounted in front of the entire aperture can show photosphere, spots and faculae, which change with solar activity.
sun.observing_notes: Never observe the Sun without a certified, intact solar filter mounted securely over the full aperture; never use eyepiece-mounted solar filters. Remove or cap the finder and inspect the filter before every session.
sun.best_seen: Daytime, using a certified full-aperture solar filter
sun.curiosity_text: The Sun does not rotate like a rigid body: being plasma, it completes one rotation in about 25 Earth days at the equator and in about 36 days at the poles. For this reason the length of its day depends on the latitude observed.

moon.short_description: The Moon is the most familiar target in the sky, but it changes face every night. The best moment is not the full phase: along the terminator, where light and shadow meet, craters, mountains and seas gain prominence. Even a small instrument shows real details and allows you to follow how the lighting transforms the landscape from one evening to the next.
moon.observing_notes: Look especially near the First and Last Quarters; along the terminator use moderate magnification and, if necessary, a moon filter.
moon.curiosity_text: The Moon always shows almost the same face because rotation and revolution have the same duration. The hidden face remained unknown until 1959, when the Soviet probe Luna 3 transmitted its first images.

mercury.short_description: Mercury is a challenge more than a spectacle. It always stays close to the Sun and allows short windows, low on the horizon, just before sunrise or just after sunset. In the telescope it appears small and often flickering, but being able to intercept its phase is a satisfaction for an attentive observer. Timing is more important than the instrument's aperture.
mercury.observing_notes: You need a clear horizon and maximum caution: never aim close to the Sun.
mercury.curiosity_text: On Mercury a solar day lasts 176 Earth days, double its year. It is the effect of the 3:2 resonance: the planet makes three rotations every two orbits around the Sun.

venus.short_description: Venus dominates twilight with an almost unreal brightness. Through a telescope it shows no surface detail because it is covered by dense clouds, but it reveals elegant phases similar to the Moon's. It is also an excellent urban target: its value lies in following how its shape and apparent diameter change over the months. When high in the sky, it handles moderate magnification well.
venus.observing_notes: Observe it when it is high in the sky; a neutral-density or colored filter can make the view more comfortable.
venus.best_seen: Dusk or dawn according to elongation
venus.curiosity_text: Venus rotates in the opposite direction to most planets and takes longer to spin than to complete an orbit. On the planet, therefore, the sidereal day is longer than the year.

mars.short_description: Mars is a planet of patience. In periods far from the opposition it may seem like just a small orange disk, but when it approaches the Earth it becomes alive: polar caps, dark areas and atmospheric variations can appear at times. Seeing decides almost everything. It's one of those targets that rewards those who come back to watch it several times in the same season.
mars.observing_notes: Use medium or high magnifications only with stable seeing; colored filters can improve contrast.
mars.curiosity_text: Olympus Mons, on Mars, is the largest volcano in the Solar System: its base would occupy a region comparable to Poland, and its summit rises more than twice as high as Everest relative to the mean Martian surface.

jupiter.short_description: Jupiter is the most dynamic planet for an amateur telescope. The equatorial bands change appearance, the Great Red Spot rotates in and out of the disk, and the Galilean satellites build a different configuration every evening. Even small instruments immediately show something real and changing. It's the ideal target when you want to see a living planet, not just a bright light.
jupiter.observing_notes: Wait for it to clear the horizon well; stable seeing and medium magnifications give more than maximum magnifications.
jupiter.best_seen: When it exceeds 30 degrees in altitude
jupiter.curiosity_text: Jupiter has the shortest day of the planets, less than ten hours. The very rapid rotation crushes the globe at the poles and drags cloud systems such as the Great Red Spot, a storm observed for centuries.

saturn.short_description: Saturn is the planet that most often turns an ordinary evening into a memory. The rings are visible even with small telescopes and make the planet unmistakable; with good seeing and sufficient aperture you can see the shadow of the rings, the Cassini Division and some satellites, first and foremost Titan. The visibility of details changes with atmospheric stability and the apparent inclination of the rings.
saturn.observing_notes: Observe it near culmination and gradually increase: Cassini Division requires stable seeing, good focus and adequate aperture.
saturn.best_seen: When it exceeds 25 degrees in altitude
saturn.curiosity_text: The average density of Saturn is lower than that of water. Its rings, although extending for hundreds of thousands of kilometres, are mainly composed of countless fragments of ice and are surprisingly thin.

uranus.short_description: Uranus impresses not with details, but with awareness of what you are observing. In the telescope it appears as a small blue-green disk, elegant and almost perfectly regular. It is the first planet discovered in the modern era and one of the strangest worlds in the Solar System, with its rotation axis tilted by almost 98 degrees. Distinguishing it from the stars is already a notable observational satisfaction.
uranus.observing_notes: Precise aiming is needed; look for color and the tiny disk instead of surface details.
uranus.curiosity_text: Uranus rotates almost lying on the orbital plane, with an axial inclination of about 98 degrees. During its 84 Earth year, each pole can remain lit or dark for about 21 years.

neptune.short_description: Neptune is a subtle and remote target. At the eyepiece it appears as a tiny blue disk that can remain almost stellar in small instruments, but knowing that the light comes from the outermost major planet in the Solar System gives the observation a particular sense of scale. The real achievement is identifying it with certainty and distinguishing it from the field stars.
neptune.observing_notes: Use an updated chart or accurate aiming, then increase the magnification to verify that a small disk remains instead of a star point.
neptune.curiosity_text: Neptune was spotted in 1846 after being predicted mathematically from perturbations in the orbit of Uranus. Although it receives little solar energy, the fastest winds in the Solar System blow through its atmosphere.

messier-M1.short_description: M1, the Crab Nebula, is the remnant of the supernova observed in 1054 in the constellation Taurus. At the eyepiece it is a faint oval blob, lacking the stringy appearance shown by photographs, but directly connecting the observer to the explosive death of a star. Dark skies and patience make a greater difference than magnification.
messier-M1.observing_notes: Use low or medium magnification, averted vision, and a clear sky; a UHC filter can help moderately, while OIII is not always the best choice.
messier-M1.curiosity_text: At the heart of the Crab Nebula remains a neutron star the size of a city. It rotates about thirty times a second and feeds the nebula's glow with a wind of relativistic particles.

messier-M2.short_description: M2 is a globular cluster in Aquarius. It is an ancient and compact globular, far from the plane of the Milky Way; it first appears as a dense stain, then slowly reveals the grainy edge.
messier-M2.observing_notes: For M2, with integrated magnitude 6.5, use the 16′ diameter as a reference as you search for the first resolved stars.
messier-M2.curiosity_text: M2 collects about 150,000 stars in an ancient sphere, formed approximately 13 billion years ago. Its densest stars occupy a volume that, on a galactic scale, is extremely compact.

messier-M3.short_description: M3 is one of the largest and richest globular clusters in the northern sky and contains an exceptionally large population of variable stars. At low magnification it shows a bright nucleus immersed in a round halo; with medium apertures the edge begins to resolve into a dense graininess. It's a great example of how the resolution gradually increases from the edge towards the center.
messier-M3.observing_notes: Center it at low magnification, then increase magnification until the peripheral stars begin to separate without making the core too dark.
messier-M3.curiosity_text: More than 270 variable stars have been cataloged in M3, an exceptional number for a globular cluster. Many are RR Lyrae, standard candles crucial for measuring distances within the Milky Way.

messier-M4.short_description: M4 is one of the closest globular clusters to the Solar System and is located just west of Antares. It is less concentrated than many other globulars and, with sufficient aperture, displays a characteristic bar of stars crossing the central region. Its low altitude above the horizon from many northern locations can limit observing performance.
messier-M4.observing_notes: Look for it near Antares when it culminates; use medium magnifications to recognize the central bar and resolve the periphery.
messier-M4.curiosity_text: M4 hosts the PSR B1620-26 system, where a pulsar and a white dwarf are orbited by a planet nicknamed Methuselah. Its estimated age, over 12 billion years, makes it one of the oldest planets known.

messier-M5.short_description: M5 (Rose Cluster) is a globular cluster in Serpens. It is one of the most beautiful globulars for amateur telescopes: bright, large and capable of transforming from a puff to a grainy star field.
messier-M5.observing_notes: In M5 (Rose Cluster) look for the transition between nucleus and halo along all 23′ of the diameter, without relying on magnitude 5.6 alone.
messier-M5.curiosity_text: The stars of M5 formed over 12 billion years ago, but the cluster also contains apparently younger blue stars. They are blue stragglers, rejuvenated by mergers or transfers of matter between companions.

messier-M6.short_description: M6 (Butterfly Cluster) is an open cluster in Scorpius. The nickname Butterfly Cluster is not accidental: the brightest stars draw an open and light figure, very pleasant at low magnification.
messier-M6.observing_notes: For M6 (Butterfly Cluster), 25′ across and integrated magnitude 4.2, choose a field that leaves a margin of sky around the cluster before increasing magnification.
messier-M6.curiosity_text: The silhouette of M6 resembles a butterfly, but its most notable color contrast is BM Scorpii: an orange giant that stands out among the blue and younger stars of the cluster.

messier-M7.short_description: M7 (Ptolemy's Cluster) is an open cluster in Scorpius. It has been known since ancient times and fills the field with obvious stellar richness; low on the horizon, it becomes magnificent only with an unobstructed southern horizon and transparent skies.
messier-M7.observing_notes: In M7 (Ptolemy's Cluster) the integrated magnitude 3.3 does not describe the faintest stars: it uses the 80′ diameter to set the initial field.
messier-M7.curiosity_text: M7 was already described by Ptolemy in the 2nd century as a nebulosity near the sting of Scorpio. It is the southernmost Messier object and one of the few with such ancient observational evidence.

messier-M8.short_description: M8 (Lagoon Nebula) is a nebula with star cluster in Sagittarius. The Lagoon is a true star-forming region: young stars, bright gas and dark structures coexist in the same field.
messier-M8.observing_notes: On M8 (Lagoon Nebula), integrated magnitude 4.6, protect dark adaptation and evaluate edge, center and overlapping stars separately.
messier-M8.curiosity_text: Inside the Lagoon, the region called the Hourglass Nebula is sculpted primarily by the young massive star Herschel 36. Radiation and stellar winds are eroding the clouds from which new stars continue to be born.

messier-M9.short_description: M9 is a globular cluster in Ophiuchus. Projected toward the center of the Milky Way, it often appears against rich star fields in a challenging area of the sky.
messier-M9.observing_notes: With M9, integrated magnitude 7.7, record central concentration and degree of peripheral resolution separately.
messier-M9.curiosity_text: M9 is located unusually close to the galactic center. The Milky Way's gravity has deformed its shape, making it less spherical than many other globulars observed in the outer regions of the halo.

messier-M10.short_description: M10 is a globular cluster in Ophiuchus. It makes an ideal pair with M12 in Ophiuchus: it is more compact and performs best when magnification begins to separate the outer edge. Averted viewing shows the extent of the halo, while medium magnification helps capture the texture of the outer regions.
messier-M10.observing_notes: To evaluate M10, with integrated magnitude 6.6, compare the 20′ profile at two magnifications and keep the one that does not extinguish the halo.
messier-M10.curiosity_text: M10 contains numerous blue stragglers, stars that appear too hot and bright for the age of the cluster. Collisions and exchanges of matter in binary systems may have rekindled their evolution.

messier-M11.short_description: M11, the Wild Duck Cluster, is one of the richest and most compact open clusters in the Messier catalogue. At low magnification it can almost look like a grainy cloud; by increasing the power it transforms into a crowd of stars crowded around a brighter component. Its density makes it appear very different from more sparse open clusters.
messier-M11.observing_notes: Use a medium field first to capture the compact shape, then zoom in to resolve the star texture.
messier-M11.curiosity_text: The name Wild Duck Cluster comes from a V-shaped arrangement of the brightest stars, described in the nineteenth century. Behind that shape, M11 is one of the richest and most compact open clusters known.

messier-M12.short_description: M12 is a globular cluster in Ophiuchus. It is less concentrated and more open than M10; modern studies suggest that it lost many low-mass stars during repeated passages through the Galaxy.
messier-M12.observing_notes: In M12, which extends 16′ and has an integrated magnitude of 6.7, note at what magnification the periphery changes from a uniform halo to a grainy texture.
messier-M12.curiosity_text: M12 appears to have lost many low-mass stars. During repeated passages through the Milky Way's disk, galactic tides may have stripped as many as a million low-mass stars from the cluster.

messier-M13.short_description: M13, the Great Hercules Cluster, is the most famous globular in the northern sky. Even in small instruments it appears as a well-focused luminous sphere; with medium apertures and good seeing the periphery resolves itself into countless stars and thin dark chains can emerge, including the so-called Propeller. It is one of the best targets for understanding how aperture, focus and patience matter.
messier-M13.observing_notes: Center at low magnification and increase magnification progressively; look for resolution at the edge first and only then for finer structures in the core.
messier-M13.curiosity_text: In 1974 the Arecibo radio telescope sent an encoded message about life on Earth towards M13. By the time the signal reaches the cluster area, in about 25,000 years, M13 will have already moved along its orbit.

messier-M14.short_description: M14 is a globular cluster in Ophiuchus. It is less immediate than the more famous globulars, but contains an enormous stellar population; It requires darkness and patience to get out of the sky.
messier-M14.observing_notes: For M14, with integrated magnitude 7.6, use the 11′ diameter as a reference as you search for the first resolved stars.
messier-M14.curiosity_text: In 1938 a nova exploded in M14, but no one reported it live. It was only recognized in 1964, by comparing archival photographic plates taken decades earlier.

messier-M15.short_description: M15 (Great Pegasus Cluster) is a globular cluster in Pegasus. It has one of the most concentrated nuclei among Messier globulars, so dense that it appears almost pinpoint-like before the rim opens up into stars.
messier-M15.observing_notes: With M15 (Great Pegasus Cluster), integrated magnitude 6.2, record central concentration and degree of peripheral resolution separately.
messier-M15.curiosity_text: M15 contains Pease 1, the first planetary nebula identified within a globular cluster. It is a very rare find because this stellar phase lasts only a short time compared to the multi-billion-year age of the system.

messier-M16.short_description: M16 (Eagle Nebula) is an emission nebula with a star cluster in Serpens. The Eagle Nebula is famous for the Pillars of Creation photographed by Hubble, but at the eyepiece the cluster is often more evident than the nebulosity.
messier-M16.observing_notes: For M16 (Eagle Nebula), integrated magnitude 6.4, alternate between direct and averted vision while keeping the same exit pupil so the comparison remains reliable.
messier-M16.curiosity_text: The Pillars of Creation are towers of gas and dust within M16, several light years long. The 1995 Hubble images made them iconic, but the columns are also incubators subjected to the erosion of newborn stars.

messier-M17.short_description: M17 (Omega, Swan, Horseshoe, Lobster, or Checkmark Nebula) is an emission nebula with a star cluster in Sagittarius. The Omega Nebula, or Swan, is among the most recognizable summer nebulae: a bright bar that takes shape with a filter and dark sky.
messier-M17.observing_notes: For M17, record the effects of the filter and magnification separately; its integrated magnitude is 6.0 and its reference extent is 11′.
messier-M17.curiosity_text: The bright part of M17 is only a small portion of a much larger molecular cloud. The young cluster hidden inside illuminates and excavates the gas, creating the shape of the Swan visible from Earth.

messier-M18.short_description: M18 (Black Swan Cluster) is an open cluster in Sagittarius. It is a small and discrete cluster, often observed in transit between M17 and M24; its value lies in the very rich context of Sagittarius.
messier-M18.observing_notes: For M18 (Black Swan Cluster), which extends 9.8′ and has an integrated magnitude of 7.5, choose a field that leaves a margin of sky around the cluster before increasing magnification.
messier-M18.curiosity_text: M18 is a very young cluster, born about 30 million years ago. Its few dozen stars show how quickly an open cluster can disperse under the action of the Galaxy and gravitational encounters.

messier-M19.short_description: M19 is a globular cluster in Ophiuchus. It is a globular with a slightly elongated shape, more interesting than it seems at first glance when the seeing allows you to increase the magnification.
messier-M19.observing_notes: For M19 the magnitude 6.8 is integrated: compare core and edge without expecting the same brightness from individual stars.
messier-M19.curiosity_text: M19 is the flattest globular in the Messier catalogue. Part of the effect may be due to interstellar dust, but strong tides from the nearby galactic center also contribute to its unusual shape.

messier-M20.short_description: M20, the Trifid Nebula, is a region in Sagittarius that combines emission and reflection nebulosity, dark lanes, and a young star cluster. It is a difficult visual target, but under a good sky it has a unique appearance.
messier-M20.observing_notes: On M20 (Trifid Nebula), integrated magnitude 6.3, protect dark adaptation and evaluate edge, center and overlapping stars separately.
messier-M20.curiosity_text: M20 brings together in the same field a red emission nebula, a blue reflection region and lanes of dark dust. The three bands that dissect its center inspired John Herschel to name it the Trifid Nebula.

messier-M21.short_description: M21 (Webb's Cross Cluster) is an open cluster in Sagittarius. It is the small stellar companion of the Trifid, less famous but useful for giving breathing space to the field and completing the M20 area.
messier-M21.observing_notes: Use the 14′ extent as a scale to recognize M21 (Webb's Cross Cluster); at integrated magnitude 6.5, note how many components emerge by switching to medium magnification.
messier-M21.curiosity_text: The stars of M21 are only about 4.6 million years old: on an astronomical scale the cluster is almost newborn. It does not yet contain red giants, because none of its stars have had time to reach that stage.

messier-M22.short_description: M22 is one of the brightest and most spectacular globular clusters visible from mid-northern latitudes. It is large, relatively loosely concentrated, and easier to resolve than many similar clusters, especially when high above the horizon. In a medium-aperture telescope it can fill the field with stars and shows a less compact core than M13.
messier-M22.observing_notes: Observe it near culmination at medium magnification; its broad, rich outer regions deserve a field of view that is not too narrow.
messier-M22.curiosity_text: M22 was recognized by Abraham Ihle in 1665 and is the first globular cluster discovered. Much later it was discovered that it also contains a rare planetary nebula and hints of multiple stellar generations.

messier-M23.short_description: M23 is an open cluster in Sagittarius. It is a large and rich cluster, immersed in the summer Milky Way; It looks better when you leave space around it instead of pushing it too hard with enlargements.
messier-M23.observing_notes: For M23, with integrated magnitude 5.5, compare richness and concentration while keeping the entire 35′ extent visible.
messier-M23.curiosity_text: M23 includes about 150 stars spread over an area larger than the full Moon. The dust in front of the cluster attenuates and reddens its light, modifying the colors that reach us.

messier-M24.short_description: M24 (Small Sagittarius Star Cloud) is a stellar cloud in the Milky Way in Sagittarius. It is not a single cluster but a stellar cloud, a bright window towards the internal regions of the Galaxy. It is intended for binoculars and low magnifications.
messier-M24.observing_notes: Prefer binoculars or very low magnification: the value is the breadth of the star cloud, not the minute detail.
messier-M24.curiosity_text: M24 is not a true cluster: it is a relatively clear window into the galactic dust. Through this gap we observe a deep stretch of the arm of Sagittarius, crowded with thousands of overlapping stars.

messier-M25.short_description: M25 is an open cluster in Sagittarius. It is a bright and relaxing open cluster, with enough scattered stars to immediately draw a structure; a Cepheid variable also stands out in the field.
messier-M25.observing_notes: In M25 the integrated magnitude 4.6 does not describe the faintest stars: it uses the 36′ diameter to set the initial field.
messier-M25.curiosity_text: M25 hosts U Sagittarii, a Cepheid variable whose pulsating rhythm reveals its true brightness. Stars like this have made it possible to build the scale of cosmic distances.

messier-M26.short_description: M26 is an open cluster in Scutum. It is compact and partially affected by interstellar dust, so it appears more delicate than other clusters in Scutum. The observational pleasure lies in separating the group from the stellar background and recognizing how the brightest stars define its structure.
messier-M26.observing_notes: M26 is about 14′ wide and has integrated magnitude 8.0; examine the cluster as a whole before evaluating its closest stellar pairs.
messier-M26.curiosity_text: The center of M26 appears strangely poor in stars. It is not necessarily empty: a cloud of interstellar dust between us and the cluster could hide its central region.

messier-M27.short_description: M27, the Dumbbell Nebula, is one of the largest and brightest planetary nebulae in the sky. The central part resembles a dumbbell or an hourglass, while under dark skies the outer halo makes the shape more oval. It responds well to nebular filters and tolerates different magnifications, making it a very informative target.
messier-M27.observing_notes: Start at low magnification to see its full extent, then try UHC and OIII and increase magnification moderately to study the central area.
messier-M27.curiosity_text: Discovered by Messier in 1764, M27 was the first planetary nebula ever identified. The name has nothing to do with planets: it describes the rounded appearance that these star shells showed in early telescopes.

messier-M28.short_description: M28 is a globular cluster in Sagittarius. It is a compact globular near the heart of Sagittarius; less scenic than M22, but interesting for its density and the surrounding star field.
messier-M28.observing_notes: To evaluate M28, with integrated magnitude 6.8, compare the 11.2′ profile at two magnifications and keep the one that does not extinguish the halo.
messier-M28.curiosity_text: In 1987 M28 became the first globular cluster in which a millisecond pulsar was discovered. The neutron star rotates hundreds of times per second, accelerated in the past by the transfer of matter from a companion.

messier-M29.short_description: M29 (Cooling Tower Cluster) is an open cluster in Cygnus. It is small and a little hidden by the dust of the Swan; it doesn't impress in terms of number of stars, but it is in a very pleasant summer region to explore.
messier-M29.observing_notes: For M29 (Cooling Tower Cluster), with integrated magnitude 7.1, compare richness and concentration while keeping the entire 7′ extent visible.
messier-M29.curiosity_text: Swan dust obscures M29 so irregularly that its distance and age have long remained uncertain. Without that absorption, several of its stars would appear many times brighter.

messier-M30.short_description: M30 (Jellyfish Cluster) is a globular cluster in Capricornus. It is a compact, low globular, with a bright core and stellar tails that become visible only when the sky cooperates.
messier-M30.observing_notes: In M30 (Jellyfish Cluster), 12′ long and with integrated magnitude 7.2, note at what magnification the periphery changes from a uniform halo to a grainy texture.
messier-M30.curiosity_text: In M30 there are two distinct sequences of blue stragglers. One appears to be produced by stellar collisions during core collapse, the other by the transfer of matter in binary systems.

messier-M31.short_description: M31, the Andromeda Galaxy, is the closest large spiral to the Milky Way and the most distant object normally visible to the naked eye. Binoculars and small telescopes show above all the bright core and an elongated halo much larger than the field; under dark skies, dust bands and satellite galaxies M32 and M110 appear. Its true size is best appreciated at low magnifications.
messier-M31.observing_notes: Use binoculars or the widest field available; look for M32 and M110 and, in dark skies, follow the dust bands on the northwestern side.
messier-M31.curiosity_text: The first known description of M31 dates back to al-Sufi's Book of Fixed Stars, in 964, where it appears as a small cloud. It is the oldest written testimony of a galaxy outside the Milky Way.

messier-M32.short_description: M32 (Andromeda Satellite #1) is a dwarf elliptical galaxy in Andromeda. It is the small elliptical companion of Andromeda: in the M31 field it appears as a compact nucleus, almost a swollen star, but it is an autonomous galaxy.
messier-M32.observing_notes: For M32 (Andromeda Satellite #1), with integrated magnitude 8.1, note orientation and core-to-halo ratio before looking for fainter structures.
messier-M32.curiosity_text: M32 may be the surviving nucleus of a once-larger galaxy. Close encounters with Andromeda would have stripped away much of its outer stars, leaving an unusually compact system.

messier-M33.short_description: M33 (Triangulum/Pinwheel Galaxy) is a spiral galaxy in Triangulum. The Triangulum Galaxy is large and nearby, but its light is distributed over a huge area. With dark skies it becomes one of the most beautiful challenges at low magnification.
messier-M33.observing_notes: The profile of M33 (Triangulum/Pinwheel Galaxy), integrated magnitude 5.7, covers approximately 70.8′ × 41.7′: protect dark adaptation and check the edges with averted vision.
messier-M33.curiosity_text: NGC 604, in an arm of M33, is one of the largest star-forming regions of the Local Group. It is about a hundred times larger than the Orion Nebula and contains hundreds of young massive stars.

messier-M34.short_description: M34 (Spiral Cluster) is an open cluster in Perseus. It's a large, airy open cluster, perfect for going from binoculars to telescope without losing a sense of the star field.
messier-M34.observing_notes: For M34 (Spiral Cluster), with integrated magnitude 5.5, start with a field wider than 35′; only narrow it if component separation improves.
messier-M34.curiosity_text: M34 was probably observed by Giovanni Battista Hoggi before 1654, over a century before its inclusion in Messier's catalogue. It is one of several cases in which early discoveries were independently rediscovered.

messier-M35.short_description: M35 (Shoe-Buckle Cluster) is an open cluster in Gemini. It is one of the most beautiful winter clusters: large, bright and full of stars. Next door, with larger openings, you can glimpse the more remote NGC 2158.
messier-M35.observing_notes: For M35 (Shoe-Buckle Cluster), with integrated magnitude 5.3, compare richness and concentration while keeping the entire 28′ extent visible.
messier-M35.curiosity_text: In the same field as M35 is NGC 2158, much further away and about ten times older. The comparison immediately shows how distance and evolution change the density and apparent color of two open clusters.

messier-M36.short_description: M36 (Pinwheel Cluster) is an open cluster in Auriga. It is the most compact of the Auriga trio, bright and easy to recognize. It works well as a first step in a winter cluster scan.
messier-M36.observing_notes: For M36 (Pinwheel Cluster), 12′ across and integrated magnitude 6.3, choose a field that leaves a margin of sky around the cluster before increasing magnification.
messier-M36.curiosity_text: Among the three large open clusters in Auriga, M36 is the youngest. Its brightest stars are only about 25 million years old and have not yet evolved into numerous red giants.

messier-M37.short_description: M37 (Salt and Pepper Cluster) is an open cluster in Auriga. It is the richest and finest of the Auriga clusters: many tiny stars, a dense center and a deeper sensation than neighboring M36 and M38.
messier-M37.observing_notes: In M37 (Salt and Pepper Cluster) the integrated magnitude 6.2 does not describe the fainter stars: it uses the 24′ diameter to set the initial field.
messier-M37.curiosity_text: M37 is the richest of the three Auriga Messier clusters and contains several red giants. Their presence signals a greater age than the nearby M36, dominated by young blue stars.

messier-M38.short_description: M38 (Starfish Cluster) is an open cluster in Auriga. It has a large, irregular structure, often described as a starfish. It is less concentrated than M37, but very pleasant in wide fields.
messier-M38.observing_notes: With M38 (Starfish Cluster), about 21′ wide and with integrated magnitude 7.4, first check the entire profile of the cluster and only then evaluate the closest pairs.
messier-M38.curiosity_text: Not far from M38 appears NGC 1907, smaller and more compact. Measurements of their motions indicate that the two clusters are crossing the same region without having originated as a bonded pair.

messier-M39.short_description: M39 (Pyramid Cluster) is an open cluster in Cygnus. It is a scattered cluster in Cygnus, almost more binocular-like than telescope-like. Its charm is simplicity: a few bright stars in a very rich summer area.
messier-M39.observing_notes: Use the 29′ extension as a scale to recognize M39 (Pyramid Cluster); at integrated magnitude 4.6, note how many components emerge by switching to medium magnification.
messier-M39.curiosity_text: M39 is so close and dispersed that it only gathers around thirty confirmed members in a very large field. Its triangular shape emerges better at low magnification than in a narrow telescope.

messier-M40.short_description: M40 (Winnecke 4) is an optical double in Ursa Major. It's a historical curiosity from the catalogue: an apparent pair of stars, not a deep-sky object. It is worth observing precisely to understand Messier's original logic.
messier-M40.observing_notes: Use low or medium magnification and treat it as a historical curiosity rather than a deep sky target.
messier-M40.curiosity_text: M40 is neither a nebula nor a cluster, but an optical pair of unbound stars. Messier recorded it by looking for a nebula reported by Hevelius which, in that position, probably did not exist.

messier-M41.short_description: M41 (Little Beehive Cluster) is an open cluster in Canis Major. Below Sirius, M41 is a bright and easy cluster, already pleasing with small instruments. The bright stars make it one of the best quick winter targets.
messier-M41.observing_notes: For M41 (Little Beehive Cluster), with integrated magnitude 4.5, compare richness and concentration while keeping the entire 38′ extent visible.
messier-M41.curiosity_text: M41 could be the celestial spot described by Aristotle around 325 BC. If the identification is correct, it would be one of the star clusters with the oldest documented observations.

messier-M42.short_description: M42, the Great Orion Nebula, is the most spectacular star-forming region readily visible from the Northern Hemisphere. Even from a city it shows a bright core around the Trapezium; under dark skies, wings, arcs, and dark regions extend far beyond the center. It offers detail at both low and high magnification.
messier-M42.observing_notes: Start without a filter to observe the Trapezium, then try UHC or OIII at low magnification to follow the faintest wings.
messier-M42.curiosity_text: The Trapezium, a group of very young massive stars, shines in the center of M42. Their radiation ionizes the surrounding gas and is simultaneously illuminating and eroding the cloud that generated them.

messier-M43.short_description: M43 (De Mairan's Nebula) is an emission nebula in Orion. It is the small nebular region next to M42, separated by a dark band, and is best appreciated in comparison with the Great Orion Nebula.
messier-M43.observing_notes: Observe it together with M42: the comparison between the two regions makes the structure of the nebula more readable.
messier-M43.curiosity_text: M43 is physically part of the large Orion cloud, but a band of dust visually separates it from M42. The star NU Orionis illuminates this portion as an autonomous center.

messier-M44.short_description: M44, the Beehive Cluster, is a large, nearby open cluster, visible to the naked eye as a bright patch under a dark sky. Binoculars transform it into a broad field of scattered stars, with pairs and small groups spread over an area larger than the full Moon. A long-focal-length telescope risks showing only part of it.
messier-M44.observing_notes: Prefer very wide-field binoculars or telescope; keep the entire cluster in the field of view.
messier-M44.curiosity_text: Galileo pointed his telescope at M44 in 1609 and resolved the naked-eye nebulosity into about forty stars. It was an early demonstration that many spots in the sky were stellar populations.

messier-M45.short_description: M45, the Pleiades, is a young and nearby open cluster, dominated by very bright blue stars. To the naked eye it shows the well-known small cluster; dozens of components appear through binoculars and the whole takes on a remarkable depth. The reflection nebulosity around the main stars is photographic and, visually, requires excellent sky and great transparency.
messier-M45.observing_notes: Observe them with binoculars or very low magnification; Don't use nebular filters and look for faint nebulosity only under a very clear sky.
messier-M45.curiosity_text: In Japan the Pleiades are Subaru, a name also adopted by the car manufacturer and represented in its logo. The blue nebulosity is not the cluster's natal remnant: it is dust that the stars are passing through.

messier-M46.short_description: M46 is an open cluster in Puppis. It is a rich cluster with a perspective surprise: the planetary nebula NGC 2438 appears in the field as a small ghost ring. At the eyepiece, the overall pattern of the group matters most: density, chains, voids and differences in brightness emerge better by keeping a bit of sky around.
messier-M46.observing_notes: For M46, with integrated magnitude 6.0, start with a field wider than 22.8′; only narrow it if component separation improves.
messier-M46.curiosity_text: The planetary nebula NGC 2438 seems immersed in M46, but it is only a perspective alignment: it is much closer to us. It's a particularly compelling example of hidden depth in a two-dimensional field.

messier-M47.short_description: M47 is an open cluster in Puppis. It's more open and bright than M46, less dense but immediate. Together they form a perfect pair for comparing two very different clusters. The observational pleasure lies in separating the group from the stellar background and recognizing how the brightest stars define its structure.
messier-M47.observing_notes: For M47, with integrated magnitude 4.4, compare richness and concentration while keeping the entire 30′ extent visible.
messier-M47.curiosity_text: M47 was considered lost for over a century due to a sign error in the coordinates published by Messier. The cluster was recognized again only when its observation path was reconstructed.

messier-M48.short_description: M48 is an open cluster in Hydra. It is large, bright, and often overlooked. At low magnification it shows a broad, loose structure that is well suited to winter or spring skies.
messier-M48.observing_notes: For M48, 30′ across and integrated magnitude 5.5, choose a field that leaves a margin of sky around the cluster before increasing magnification.
messier-M48.curiosity_text: M48 also became a lost object: an incorrect declination moved it about five degrees. The modern correction identified the cluster as NGC 2548.

messier-M49.short_description: M49 is an elliptical galaxy in Virgo. It is a large elliptical of the Virgo cluster: visually it is a soft light without details, but it represents a gigantic stellar city.
messier-M49.observing_notes: For M49, with integrated magnitude 8.4, use the dimensions 10.2′ × 8.3′ to choose the field and compare how far the halo extends beyond the core.
messier-M49.curiosity_text: M49 was the first galaxy of the Virgo Cluster discovered by Messier in 1771. It is an elliptical giant with a vast system of globular clusters and a central supermassive black hole.

messier-M50.short_description: M50 (Heart-Shaped Cluster) is an open cluster in Monoceros. It is a compact open cluster, often described as having a heart shape. It's not famous, but it offers clean and pleasant viewing.
messier-M50.observing_notes: With M50 (Heart-Shaped Cluster), about 16′ wide and with integrated magnitude 5.9, first check the entire profile of the cluster and only then evaluate the closest pairs.
messier-M50.curiosity_text: A very obvious red giant contrasts with the blue-white stars of M50. The ensemble was nicknamed the Heart Cluster for a shape that depends above all on the brightest members.

messier-M51.short_description: M51, the Whirlpool Galaxy, is a spiral seen almost face-on interacting with its companion NGC 5195. In small instruments, two nuclei immersed in a common halo can be distinguished; under dark skies and with medium apertures the arms can appear as arcing variations in brightness and the bridge towards the companion becomes discernible. It is one of the best targets for attempting visual spiral structure.
messier-M51.observing_notes: Locate the two nuclei first, then use averted vision and medium magnifications to look for arches and a bright bridge.
messier-M51.curiosity_text: In 1845 Lord Rosse recognized M51 as the first spiral structure observed in a nebula. At the time it was not yet clear that those spirals were galaxies outside the Milky Way.

messier-M52.short_description: M52 (Scorpion Cluster) is an open cluster in Cassiopeia. It is a rich cluster near Cassiopeia, beautiful precisely because it is dense and minute. It requires some attention to separate it from the Milky Way's star field.
messier-M52.observing_notes: For M52 (Scorpion Cluster), with integrated magnitude 7.3, start with a field wider than 13′; only narrow it if component separation improves.
messier-M52.curiosity_text: M52 is in the same line of sight as the Bubble Nebula, but the two objects are not necessarily close in space. The strong extinction of Cassiopeia makes even the precise distance of the cluster uncertain.

messier-M53.short_description: M53 is a globular cluster in Coma Berenices. It is a remote and compact globular, close to the star Diadem. It's not as spectacular as M13, but it has a quiet elegance and a very clear core.
messier-M53.observing_notes: In M53 look for the transition between nucleus and halo along all 13′ of the diameter, without relying on magnitude 7.6 alone.
messier-M53.curiosity_text: M53 is one of the globulars furthest from the center of the Milky Way and has very few heavy elements. Its composition therefore retains a chemical signature from the early ages of the Galaxy.

messier-M54.short_description: M54 is a globular cluster in Sagittarius. It is a particular globular because it is associated with the Sagittarius dwarf galaxy: by observing it you are looking at an object linked to a small galaxy colliding with ours.
messier-M54.observing_notes: In M54, which extends 12′ and has an integrated magnitude of 7.6, note at what magnification the periphery changes from a uniform halo to a grainy texture.
messier-M54.curiosity_text: M54 probably does not belong to the original halo of the Milky Way: it resides in the nucleus of the Sagittarius Elliptical Dwarf Galaxy, which our Galaxy is incorporating. It is therefore a globular acquired through a merger.

messier-M55.short_description: M55 (Specter Cluster) is a globular cluster in Sagittarius. It is a large and relatively loose globular: less concentrated than many others, but very beautiful when the southern sky is clean and transparent.
messier-M55.observing_notes: For M55 (Specter Cluster) with integrated magnitude 6.3: compare core and edge without expecting the same brightness from individual stars.
messier-M55.curiosity_text: M55 has a loosely concentrated core, so its stars resolve more easily than many globulars. It also contains dozens of variables, useful for reconstructing its distance and evolution.

messier-M56.short_description: M56 is a globular cluster in Lyra, between Lyra and Cygnus in a region already rich in targets. It is a subtle globular cluster that rewards patient observation rather than a quick glance.
messier-M56.observing_notes: For M56, with integrated magnitude 8.3, use the 8.8′ diameter as a reference as you search for the first resolved stars.
messier-M56.curiosity_text: The retrograde orbit and composition of M56 suggest that it may have arrived from a small galaxy absorbed by the Milky Way. Its motion preserves the dynamic trace of that ancient merger.

messier-M57.short_description: M57, the Ring Nebula, is a compact, high-surface-brightness planetary nebula in Lyra. Even with small telescopes it appears as a tiny ring or perforated disk; as you increase the magnification the darker center becomes sharp, and the edge shows uneven brightness. The central star is much more difficult and requires a large aperture and excellent conditions.
messier-M57.observing_notes: Center at low magnification, then increase magnification when the seeing is steady; an OIII filter accentuates the ring, but the central star remains challenging.
messier-M57.curiosity_text: The Ring Nebula is not a simple flat ring. The three-dimensional reconstructions describe a structure similar to a barrel or a donut, observed almost along its axis.

messier-M58.short_description: M58 is a barred spiral galaxy in Virgo. It is a barred Virgo spiral, visually sober but interesting because it brings galactic structure into an object that is not easy to read through the eyepiece.
messier-M58.observing_notes: For M58, with integrated magnitude 9.7, compare the observed diameter to 5.9′ × 4.7′; marked differences indicate that the sky background hides the external halo.
messier-M58.curiosity_text: M58 is one of only four barred spiral galaxies in the Messier catalog. Its active core hosts a supermassive black hole that accretes matter.

messier-M59.short_description: M59 is an elliptical galaxy in Virgo. It's an elliptical of the Virgo cluster: it offers no obvious detail, but becomes significant when you observe it as part of a network of nearby galaxies in the sky.
messier-M59.observing_notes: In M59, magnitude 9.6 and dimensions 5.4′ × 3.7′ must be read together: the surface contrast determines how much of the galaxy emerges.
messier-M59.curiosity_text: M59 appears elliptical and regular, but its center contains a black hole of enormous mass compared to the galaxy. Thousands of globular clusters also orbit around it.

messier-M60.short_description: M60 is an elliptical galaxy in Virgo, next to the spiral NGC 4647. In the telescope, the pair shows how varied the Virgo Cluster's galaxy population can be.
messier-M60.observing_notes: For M60, extended 7.4′ × 6.0′, first check axis and central condensation; magnitude 8.8 alone does not express surface brightness.
messier-M60.curiosity_text: Next to M60 is M60-UCD1, an ultracompact galaxy with extreme stellar density and a disproportionate central black hole. It could be the stripped core of a larger galaxy.

messier-M61.short_description: M61 (Swelling Spiral Galaxy) is a spiral galaxy in Virgo. It is a spiral seen almost frontally, also famous for its supernovae. With dark skies it can show a strong core and a more irregular halo.
messier-M61.observing_notes: For M61 (Swelling Spiral Galaxy), with integrated magnitude 9.7, use the dimensions 6.5′ × 5.8′ to choose the field and compare how far the halo extends beyond the core.
messier-M61.curiosity_text: M61 has been the site of numerous observed supernovae, more than most Messier galaxies. Its active core and star-forming regions indicate a still very dynamic system.

messier-M62.short_description: M62 (Flickering Globular) is an asymmetric, concentrated globular cluster in Ophiuchus, near the central region of the Galaxy. Its irregular shape makes it more interesting than expected.
messier-M62.observing_notes: For M62 (Flickering Globular), with integrated magnitude 6.5, use the 15′ diameter as a reference as you search for the first resolved stars.
messier-M62.curiosity_text: The shape of M62 is visibly asymmetrical. The proximity to the galactic center subjects the cluster to intense tidal forces, which compress and deform the distribution of its stars.

messier-M63.short_description: M63 (Sunflower Galaxy) is a spiral galaxy in Canes Venatici. The Sunflower Galaxy has fragmented arms and dust lanes in deep images. At the eyepiece it appears as an oval glow with a distinctive profile.
messier-M63.observing_notes: The profile of M63 (Sunflower Galaxy), integrated magnitude 8.6, covers approximately 12.6′ × 7.2′: protect dark adaptation and check the edges with averted vision.
messier-M63.curiosity_text: A thin stream of stars envelops M63 for tens of thousands of light-years. It is the remnant of a torn and absorbed dwarf galaxy, a merger still legible on the outskirts of the Sunflower.

messier-M64.short_description: M64 (Black Eye Galaxy) is a spiral galaxy in Coma Berenices. The Black Eye Galaxy is famous for the dark band near the nucleus. In medium instruments and dark skies, detecting that contrast can become a real observational achievement.
messier-M64.observing_notes: For M64 (Black Eye Galaxy), with integrated magnitude 8.5, compare the observed diameter to 10.7′ × 5.1′; marked differences indicate that the sky background hides the external halo.
messier-M64.curiosity_text: In M64 the gas in the outer regions rotates in the opposite direction to the gas and the inner stars. This counter-rotation is probably the legacy of a small gas-rich galaxy incorporated in the past.

messier-M65.short_description: M65 (Leo Triplet) is a barred spiral galaxy in Leo. It is one of the three galaxies of the Leo Triplet. Thin and uncluttered, it is at its best when viewed alongside M66 and NGC 3628 in the same path.
messier-M65.observing_notes: In M65 (Leo Triplet), magnitude 9.3 and dimensions 8.7′ × 2.5′ must be read together: the surface contrast determines how much of the galaxy emerges.
messier-M65.curiosity_text: M65 forms the Leo Triplet with M66 and NGC 3628. Although appearing less perturbed than its companions, its disk shows deformations compatible with mutual gravitational interactions.

messier-M66.short_description: M66 (Leo Triplet) is a barred spiral galaxy in Leo. It is the most obvious component of the Leo Triplet, with a strong core and a more disturbed shape. It is a galaxy that tells of past interactions.
messier-M66.observing_notes: For M66 (Leo Triplet), extended 9.1′ × 4.2′, first check axis and central condensation; magnitude 8.9 alone does not express surface brightness.
messier-M66.curiosity_text: An arm of M66 is noticeably deformed, and the nucleus is displaced with respect to the symmetry of the disk. The nearby passage of NGC 3628 has reshaped the galaxy and triggered new star formation.

messier-M67.short_description: M67 (King Cobra or Golden Eye Cluster) is an open cluster in Cancer. It is one of the oldest and most studied open clusters, very different from the young blue clusters. To the eye it appears rich, mature and surprisingly balanced.
messier-M67.observing_notes: In M67 (King Cobra or Golden Eye Cluster) the integrated magnitude 6.1 does not describe the fainter stars: it uses the 30′ diameter to set the initial field.
messier-M67.curiosity_text: M67 is about four billion years old and has a composition similar to that of the Sun. For this reason it is a privileged laboratory for comparing the evolution of the Sun with stars born almost in the same period.

messier-M68.short_description: M68 is a globular cluster in Hydra. It is a globular in Hydra, often low and not immediate. When the southern horizon is good, it shows a compact core in a fairly solitary field.
messier-M68.observing_notes: For M68, with integrated magnitude 7.8, use the 11′ diameter as a reference as you search for the first resolved stars.
messier-M68.curiosity_text: M68 follows a very eccentric and retrograde orbit with respect to the galactic rotation. This behavior, together with the low metallicity, suggests an origin in a subsequently captured system.

messier-M69.short_description: M69 is a globular cluster in Sagittarius. It is a small globular concentrated in Sagittarius, less spectacular than M22 but interesting for its stellar population rich in heavy elements.
messier-M69.observing_notes: With M69, integrated magnitude 7.6, record central concentration and degree of peripheral resolution separately.
messier-M69.curiosity_text: M69 is among the globulars richest in heavy elements in the Messier catalogue. Its position in the galactic bulge tells of a different formation environment from the metal-poor globulars of the halo.

messier-M70.short_description: M70 is a globular cluster in Sagittarius. It is a compact and difficult globular, close to the area where comet Hale-Bopp was discovered. It is a transparent sky target, not an urban evening one.
messier-M70.observing_notes: To evaluate M70, with integrated magnitude 7.9, compare the 8′ profile at two magnifications and keep the one that does not extinguish the halo.
messier-M70.curiosity_text: Alan Hale and Thomas Bopp independently discovered comet Hale-Bopp in 1995 while observing the region near M70. The globular thus became the casual reference of one of the most famous comets of the twentieth century.

messier-M71.short_description: M71 (Angelfish Cluster) is a globular cluster in Sagitta. It is an ambiguous and fascinating object, halfway between a loose globular and a very dense cluster. In the Sagitta star field it appears as a grainy condensation.
messier-M71.observing_notes: In M71 (Angelfish Cluster) look for the transition between core and halo along the entire 7.2′ of the diameter, without relying on magnitude 8.2 alone.
messier-M71.curiosity_text: For a long time M71 was classified sometimes as an open cluster, sometimes as globular, because it is not very concentrated and relatively rich in metals. Modern measurements place it among the youngest and most unusual globulars.

messier-M72.short_description: M72 is a globular cluster in Aquarius. It is one of the weakest globulars in the Messier catalog. It doesn't immediately impress, but it is rewarding precisely because it requires method and averted vision.
messier-M72.observing_notes: In M72, which extends 6.6′ and has an integrated magnitude of 9.3, note at what magnification the periphery changes from a uniform halo to a grainy texture.
messier-M72.curiosity_text: M72 is one of the most distant globulars inserted by Messier. The great distance compresses its appearance into a faint blob, even though it actually contains a large and very ancient stellar population.

messier-M73.short_description: M73 is a small asterism in Aquarius. It's a small asterism of four stars, more curiosity than spectacle. Its presence in the catalog is a reminder of how practical and observational Messier's work was.
messier-M73.observing_notes: It is a context object: it is worth more for the history of the catalog than for visual spectacularity.
messier-M73.curiosity_text: The four stars of M73 look like a small cluster, but measured distances and motions show that they do not form a physical system. It is an asterism born from a random alignment along the line of sight.

messier-M74.short_description: M74 (Phantom Galaxy) is a spiral galaxy in Pisces. The Phantom Galaxy is large, front-facing and has low surface brightness. It looks beautiful in pictures, but in visuals it only rewards really dark skies.
messier-M74.observing_notes: For M74 (Phantom Galaxy), with integrated magnitude 9.4, note orientation and core-to-halo ratio before looking for fainter structures.
messier-M74.curiosity_text: M74 is a grand design spiral that is almost perfectly frontal, but has a very low surface brightness. This combination makes it photogenic and, at the same time, one of the most difficult Messier objects to see.

messier-M75.short_description: M75 is a globular cluster in Sagittarius. It is one of the most concentrated globulars in the catalogue, with a compact and difficult to resolve core. It seems small, but hides a remarkable density.
messier-M75.observing_notes: With M75, integrated magnitude 8.5, record central concentration and degree of peripheral resolution separately.
messier-M75.curiosity_text: M75 has one of the most concentrated nuclei among Messier globulars. The light grows rapidly towards the center, where the density of stars is much higher than in the outer halo.

messier-M76.short_description: M76 (Little Dumbbell Nebula) is a planetary nebula in Perseus. The Little Dumbbell is a demanding planetary nebula: small, weak and structured. When it emerges, however, it gives greater satisfaction than many easier objects.
messier-M76.observing_notes: For M76 (Little Dumbbell Nebula), integrated magnitude 10.1, alternate between direct and averted vision while keeping the same exit pupil so the comparison remains reliable.
messier-M76.curiosity_text: M76 has been given more names than almost any other planetary nebula: Little Dumbbell, Cork, and Butterfly. The two bright lobes are the walls of a structure expelled by a dying star.

messier-M77.short_description: M77 (Cetus A or Squid Galaxy) is a spiral galaxy in Cetus. It is an active Seyfert galaxy with an energetic core. At the eyepiece it looks like a compact spot, but physically it is a very powerful system.
messier-M77.observing_notes: In M77 (Cetus A or Squid Galaxy), magnitude 8.9 and dimensions 7.1′ × 6.0′ must be read together: the surface contrast determines how much of the galaxy emerges.
messier-M77.curiosity_text: The center of M77 is one of the closest active galactic nuclei. A supermassive black hole, hidden by a torus of dust, fuels emissions so intense that it makes the galaxy the prototype of type 2 Seyferts.

messier-M78.short_description: M78 is a diffuse nebula in Orion. It is a reflection nebula: it does not shine from ionized gas, but from the light of young stars reflected by the dust. It requires transparency rather than aggressive filters.
messier-M78.observing_notes: Transparency is crucial: observe it without narrowband filters, at low magnification, and under a dark sky.
messier-M78.curiosity_text: M78 is the brightest reflection nebula in the sky. Its dust does not emit its own light: it diffuses the blue glow of young stars and surrounds Herbig-Haro jets produced by stars still forming.

messier-M79.short_description: M79 is a globular cluster in Lepus. It is an unusual winter globular, far from the classic summer fields of the Milky Way. In Lepus, it appears compact and surprising below Orion.
messier-M79.observing_notes: For M79 the magnitude 7.7 is integrated: compare core and edge without expecting the same brightness from individual stars.
messier-M79.curiosity_text: M79 is located on the opposite side of the sky from the galactic center, an unusual location for a globular. Its orbit has fueled the hypothesis that it was acquired during a merger with a dwarf galaxy.

messier-M80.short_description: M80 is a globular cluster in Scorpius. It is a very dense globular, small but intense. With medium apertures the edge begins to sparkle while the core remains compact.
messier-M80.observing_notes: For M80, with integrated magnitude 7.3, use the 10′ diameter as a reference as you search for the first resolved stars.
messier-M80.curiosity_text: M80 is one of the densest globulars in the Milky Way. In 1860 the nova T Scorpii appeared there, which for a few days reached a brightness comparable to that of the entire cluster.

messier-M81.short_description: M81 is a large, bright and well-focused spiral galaxy in Ursa Major. At the eyepiece it shows a clear nucleus immersed in an oval halo; the arms are thin and difficult, but the contrast with nearby M82 makes the pair one of the most beautiful extragalactic fields in the sky. A wide field of view can include both galaxies.
messier-M81.observing_notes: Use low magnification to include M82, then increase magnification moderately on M81 to follow the gradient of the nucleus and the halo.
messier-M81.curiosity_text: The core of M81 contains a black hole of about 70 million solar masses. The interaction with M82 also traced long hydrogen bridges between the two galaxies and fueled new stellar activity.

messier-M82.short_description: M82, the Cigar Galaxy, is a starburst galaxy seen edge-on and perturbed by interaction with M81. The narrow disk is very bright and, with medium apertures, shows dark nodes and bands that break it into irregular sections. It is richer in visual detail than many galaxies and forms a memorable pair with M81.
messier-M82.observing_notes: View it first with M81, then use medium magnification and averted vision to look for dark lanes in the disk.
messier-M82.curiosity_text: The flyby of M81 turned M82 into a starburst galaxy. At its center, stars are born at a rate many times faster than the Milky Way's, as jets of hot gas escape from the disk.

messier-M83.short_description: M83 (Southern Pinwheel Galaxy) is a barred spiral galaxy in Hydra. The Southern Pinwheel is a large barred spiral, beautiful but low to many European observers. When it gets high enough, it is one of the most rewarding galaxies in the South.
messier-M83.observing_notes: In M83 (Southern Pinwheel Galaxy), magnitude 7.6 and dimensions 12.9′ × 11.5′ must be read together: the surface contrast determines how much of the galaxy emerges.
messier-M83.curiosity_text: M83 is a supernova factory: at least six have been observed in the last century. The numerous pink regions along the arms reveal particularly intense star formation.

messier-M84.short_description: M84 is a Virgo galaxy with a classification intermediate between elliptical and lenticular. It belongs to Markarian's Chain and is more significant in the context of the group than for detail visible in the individual galaxy.
messier-M84.observing_notes: For M84, extended 6.5′ × 5.6′, first check axis and central condensation; magnitude 9.1 alone does not express surface brightness.
messier-M84.curiosity_text: M84 lies in Markarian's Chain and hosts an active nucleus. A relativistic jet emerges from the region of its central black hole, although it is far less conspicuous than the jet from nearby M87.

messier-M85.short_description: M85 is a lenticular galaxy in Coma Berenices. It is a softly glowing lenticular galaxy in the Coma Berenices region. It does not reveal obvious detail, but it fits well into a spring galaxy hunt.
messier-M85.observing_notes: For M85, with integrated magnitude 9.1, use the dimensions 7.1′ × 5.5′ to choose the field and compare how far the halo extends beyond the core.
messier-M85.curiosity_text: M85's smooth appearance hides a history of mergers: stellar shells, dust and a relatively young central population indicate that the galaxy incorporated a companion in astronomically recent times.

messier-M86.short_description: M86 is a Virgo galaxy with a classification intermediate between elliptical and lenticular. Observing it with M84 and the other members of Markarian's Chain gives the impression of crossing an entire galaxy cluster.
messier-M86.observing_notes: For M86, with integrated magnitude 8.9, note orientation and core-to-halo ratio before looking for fainter structures.
messier-M86.curiosity_text: M86 is approaching us at hundreds of kilometers per second, despite belonging to the Virgo Cluster. Passing through the hot gas of the cluster, it leaves behind a tail of matter hundreds of thousands of light years long.

messier-M87.short_description: M87 (Virgo A) is an elliptical galaxy in Virgo. It is a gigantic elliptical galaxy, famous for the black hole photographed by the Event Horizon Telescope. Visually it is sober, but conceptually enormous.
messier-M87.observing_notes: The profile of M87 (Virgo A), integrated magnitude 8.6, covers approximately 7.2′ × 6.8′: protect dark adaptation and check the edges with averted vision.
messier-M87.curiosity_text: In 2019, M87's black hole became the first whose shadow was imaged with the Event Horizon Telescope. It has a mass of billions of Suns and powers a jet visible for thousands of light years.

messier-M88.short_description: M88 is a spiral galaxy in Coma Berenices. It is a tilted spiral of the Virgo Cluster, with a clear core. It takes a dark sky to see more than a simple oval glow.
messier-M88.observing_notes: For M88, with integrated magnitude 9.6, compare the observed diameter to 6.9′ × 3.7′; marked differences indicate that the sky background hides the external halo.
messier-M88.curiosity_text: M88 is hurtling towards the center of the Virgo Cluster along a highly elongated orbit. The pressure of the intergalactic gas begins to modify its hydrogen content and therefore the future of star formation.

messier-M89.short_description: M89 is an elliptical galaxy in Virgo. It is an almost round elliptical, not very spectacular but useful for understanding the variety of galaxies in Virgo. It is an object for systematic observation.
messier-M89.observing_notes: In M89, magnitude 9.8 and dimensions 5.1′ × 4.7′ must be read together: the surface contrast determines how much of the galaxy emerges.
messier-M89.curiosity_text: M89 looks almost like a perfect sphere, but deep photographs show very faint shells and plumes. They are scars left by small galaxies incorporated into the past.

messier-M90.short_description: M90 (Carabin Galaxy) is a spiral galaxy in Virgo. It is a large Virgo spiral with a particular motion compared to us. At the eyepiece it is delicate, but its elongated profile makes it recognizable.
messier-M90.observing_notes: For M90 (Carabin Galaxy), extended 9.5′ × 4.4′, first check axis and central condensation; magnitude 9.5 alone does not express surface brightness.
messier-M90.curiosity_text: M90 is a rare blue-shifted Messier galaxy, because it moves in our direction within the Virgo Cluster. The gas in its disk is torn apart by the pressure of the intergalactic medium.

messier-M91.short_description: M91 is a faint barred spiral galaxy in Coma Berenices and has historically been difficult to identify. Locating it confidently is already part of the satisfaction, especially under suburban skies.
messier-M91.observing_notes: For M91, with integrated magnitude 10.2, use the dimensions 5.4′ × 4.3′ to choose the field and compare how far the halo extends beyond the core.
messier-M91.curiosity_text: M91 was long one of Messier's great lost objects. An error in the reference used to calculate the coordinates was reconstructed in the 20th century, identifying it with the barred spiral NGC 4548.

messier-M92.short_description: M92 is a globular cluster in Hercules. It is a magnificent globular often overshadowed by the fame of M13. More compact and ancient in appearance, it is worth a visit whenever Hercules is up.
messier-M92.observing_notes: For M92, with integrated magnitude 6.4, use the 14′ diameter as a reference as you search for the first resolved stars.
messier-M92.curiosity_text: Due to the Earth's precession, in about 14,000 years the north celestial pole will pass within one degree of M92. The cluster will thus become a spectacular neighbor of the point around which the sky will rotate.

messier-M93.short_description: M93 (Critter Cluster) is a bright open cluster in Puppis, with a triangular or wedge shape. It's simple, but very nice at low magnifications.
messier-M93.observing_notes: Use the 10′ extent as a scale to recognize M93 (Critter Cluster); at integrated magnitude 6.0, note how many components emerge by switching to medium magnification.
messier-M93.curiosity_text: The brightest stars of M93 draw a triangular or butterfly shape. The cluster is a few hundred million years old, enough for several massive components to have already become red giants.

messier-M94.short_description: M94 (Crocodile Eye or Cat's Eye Galaxy) is a spiral galaxy in Canes Venatici. It has a very bright core surrounded by ring-like structures in deep images. At the eyepiece it is one of the easiest galaxies in Canes Venatici.
messier-M94.observing_notes: For M94 (Crocodile Eye or Cat's Eye Galaxy), with integrated magnitude 8.2, compare the observed diameter to 11.2′ × 9.1′; marked differences indicate that the sky background hides the external halo.
messier-M94.curiosity_text: In addition to the bright inner ring, M94 has a huge outer disk made up of faint spiral arms. This peripheral structure still hosts star formation, despite appearing almost like a separate ring.

messier-M95.short_description: M95 is a barred spiral galaxy in Leo. It is a barred spiral from the Leo group, subtle and not immediately obvious. It requires dark skies to stand out from its peers in the area.
messier-M95.observing_notes: In M95, magnitude 9.7 and dimensions 3.1′ × 2.9′ must be read together: the surface contrast determines how much of the galaxy emerges.
messier-M95.curiosity_text: In 2012 the supernova SN 2012aw exploded in M95. Previous images identified the progenitor as a red supergiant, directly linking a star to its final explosion.

messier-M96.short_description: M96 is a spiral galaxy in Leo. It is a bright galaxy in the Leo group, more accessible than M95. Shows obvious core and soft halo with medium instruments.
messier-M96.observing_notes: For M96, extended 7.6′ × 5.2′, first check the axis and central condensation; magnitude 9.2 alone does not express surface brightness.
messier-M96.curiosity_text: The core of M96 is not centered with the arms and the disc appears asymmetrical. The gravitational perturbations of the Leo Group, perhaps amplified by the nearby M95, have deformed its structure.

messier-M97.short_description: M97 (Owl Nebula) is a planetary nebula in Ursa Major. The Owl Nebula is a large and faint planetary: the 'eyes' are a visual challenge, but even without seeing them it remains a very characteristic target.
messier-M97.observing_notes: For M97 (Owl Nebula), with integrated magnitude 9.9, use the 3.4′ × 3.3′ dimensions to keep the entire nebulosity in the field before narrowing the field.
messier-M97.curiosity_text: The eyes of the Owl Nebula are two less dense cavities in the shell of gas. The effect depends on the orientation: we observe a three-dimensional structure shaped by the wind of the central white dwarf.

messier-M98.short_description: M98 is a spiral galaxy in Coma Berenices. It is a spiral seen nearly edge-on, long and thin. Its light is faint and diffuse, so it requires transparent skies and averted vision.
messier-M98.observing_notes: Dark skies and averted vision help follow the thin disk past the nucleus.
messier-M98.curiosity_text: M98 is blueshifted and approaching the Milky Way, unusual behavior for such a distant galaxy. Its near-edge disk is rich in dust and hydrogen, but shows signs of disruption in Virgo's environment.

messier-M99.short_description: M99 (St. Catherine's Wheel) is a nearly face-on, asymmetrical spiral galaxy in Coma Berenices. Images show spectacular arms; at the eyepiece, detecting the nucleus and halo is a realistic goal.
messier-M99.observing_notes: The profile of M99 (St. Catherine's Wheel), integrated magnitude 9.9, covers approximately 5.4′ × 4.7′: protect dark adaptation and check the edges with averted vision.
messier-M99.curiosity_text: One of M99's arms is much more extended than the others. The asymmetry may have been produced by an encounter with a nearby galaxy and by the pressure exerted by the gas from the Virgo Cluster.

messier-M100.short_description: M100 (Mirror Galaxy) is a large grand-design spiral galaxy in Coma Berenices, elegant and famous in images. At the eyepiece it is faint, but it conveys the depth of the Virgo Cluster well.
messier-M100.observing_notes: For M100 (Mirror Galaxy), with integrated magnitude 9.3, compare the observed diameter to 7.4′ × 6.3′; marked differences indicate that the sky background hides the external halo.
messier-M100.curiosity_text: The Cepheids observed by Hubble in M100 were a milestone in the project that measured the Hubble constant. This galaxy therefore contributed to calibrating the rate of expansion of the Universe.

messier-M101.short_description: M101 (Pinwheel Galaxy) is a spiral galaxy in Ursa Major. The Pinwheel Galaxy is huge and close, but with very low surface brightness. It does not forgive clear skies: when it appears, it is one of the finest visions of the Big Dipper.
messier-M101.observing_notes: In M101 (Pinwheel Galaxy), magnitude 7.9 and dimensions 28.8′ × 26.9′ must be read together: the surface contrast determines how much of the galaxy emerges.
messier-M101.curiosity_text: M101 is almost twice the size of the Milky Way and contains hundreds of billions of stars, but its disk is highly asymmetric. Encounters with companion galaxies have stretched one side of the arms.

messier-M102.short_description: M102 (Spindle Galaxy) is a lenticular galaxy in Draco. The Spindle Galaxy is thin and seen edge-on, with a dust lane that gives it an elegant appearance in images. Visually it is compact but distinct.
messier-M102.observing_notes: For M102 (Spindle Galaxy), extended 4.7′ × 1.9′, first check axis and central condensation; magnitude 9.9 alone does not express surface brightness.
messier-M102.curiosity_text: The identity of M102 is still debated because Méchain described it without reliable coordinates. The most accepted candidate is NGC 5866, a lenticular galaxy seen almost edge-on and crossed by a thin band of dust.

messier-M103.short_description: M103 is an open cluster in Cassiopeia. It's a small open cluster in Cassiopeia, easy to fit into an autumn Milky Way scan. It is not large, but has a compact and recognizable shape.
messier-M103.observing_notes: In M103 the integrated magnitude 7.4 does not describe the fainter stars: it uses the 6′ diameter to set the initial field.
messier-M103.curiosity_text: M103 contains only a few dozen confirmed members and is one of the most distant open clusters in the Messier catalog. Two red giants add a stark contrast to the dominant blue stars.

messier-M104.short_description: M104, the Sombrero Galaxy, is a spiral seen almost edge-on with a large central bulge and a clear band of dust. Even when the band is not directly visible, the bright core and very elongated profile give it a characteristic appearance. The low declination from many boreal locations makes it important to observe it near culmination.
messier-M104.observing_notes: Use medium magnification and look for asymmetry produced by the dust band along the edge of the bulge.
messier-M104.curiosity_text: Sombrero has an unusually rich system, around two thousand globular clusters: almost ten times those of the Milky Way. The dust belt hides a stellar disk inside a huge halo.

messier-M105.short_description: M105 is an elliptical galaxy in Leo. It is the largest elliptical in the Messier catalogue, in the Leone group. Visually it is simple, but it tells of a rich and compact galactic environment.
messier-M105.observing_notes: The profile of M105, integrated magnitude 9.3, covers approximately 5.4′ × 4.8′: protect dark adaptation and check the edges with averted vision.
messier-M105.curiosity_text: M105 was considered a completely dead galaxy, but deep observations found young stars and clouds of hydrogen. Even a large elliptical can therefore preserve small pockets of star formation.

messier-M106.short_description: M106 is an active spiral galaxy in Canes Venatici, known for energetic emissions and water masers. At the eyepiece it is bright and rewarding for a galaxy.
messier-M106.observing_notes: For M106, with integrated magnitude 8.4, compare the observed diameter to 18.6′ × 7.2′; marked differences indicate that the sky background hides the external halo.
messier-M106.curiosity_text: M106 shows two anomalous arms that do not follow the stellar disk. They are produced by shock waves and jets tied to the central black hole, which heat the gas as they pass through the galaxy.

messier-M107.short_description: M107 (Crucifix Cluster) is a globular cluster in Ophiuchus. It is a relatively loose globular in Ophiuchus, less dense than the more famous classics. It requires dark skies, but has a delicate and personal appearance.
messier-M107.observing_notes: In M107 (Crucifix Cluster) look for the transition between nucleus and halo along all 10′ of the diameter, without relying on magnitude 7.9 alone.
messier-M107.curiosity_text: M107 was the last Messier object discovered by Pierre Méchain and was only officially added to the catalog in 1947. With M105 and M106 he completed the modern version of the 110 objects.

messier-M108.short_description: M108 (Surfboard Galaxy) is a barred spiral galaxy in Ursa Major. The Surfboard Galaxy is a long, thin edged spiral close to the Owl Nebula in the sky. It's a nice test of averted vision.
messier-M108.observing_notes: For M108 (Surfboard Galaxy), extended 8.7′ × 2.2′, first check axis and central condensation; magnitude 10.0 alone does not express surface brightness.
messier-M108.curiosity_text: M108 is seen almost edge-on and does not show a well-defined central bulge. Its irregular disk, rich in dust and star-forming regions, contains numerous compact X-ray sources.

messier-M109.short_description: M109 is a barred spiral galaxy in Ursa Major, close to Phecda. It is not showy, but it is relatively easy to locate, and its central bar makes its structure interesting to examine.
messier-M109.observing_notes: For M109 (Vacuum Cleaner Galaxy), with integrated magnitude 9.8, use the dimensions 7.6′ × 4.7′ to choose the field and compare how far the halo extends beyond the nucleus.
messier-M109.curiosity_text: M109 is the brightest galaxy in a group that includes dozens of members. The central bar guides gas to the internal regions and helps draw a faint ring around the core.

messier-M110.short_description: M110 (Andromeda Satellite #2) is a dwarf elliptical galaxy in Andromeda. It is an elliptical companion of Andromeda, wider and more suffused than M32. In dark skies completes the view of M31 as a small system of galaxies, not as an isolated object.
messier-M110.observing_notes: For M110 (Andromeda Satellite #2), with integrated magnitude 8.5, note orientation and core-to-halo ratio before looking for fainter structures.
messier-M110.curiosity_text: Despite being classified as a dwarf elliptical, M110 contains dust and relatively young stars near the center. They are indications of recent star formation, unusual for such a regular-looking galaxy.

caldwell-C1.short_description: C1, NGC 188, is one of the oldest known open clusters and is located near the north celestial pole in Cepheus. It is rich but inconspicuous, made up of relatively faint stars distributed in a large, grainy group. Its circumpolar position makes it observable for most of the year from northern latitudes. NGC 188 covers about 14′ in the sky and has an integrated magnitude of 8.1, two data points to be read together with the background contrast.
caldwell-C1.observing_notes: Use a medium field under dark skies; increase magnification moderately to separate the many faint stars from the background.
caldwell-C1.curiosity_text: NGC 188 is about five billion years old, an exceptional age for an open cluster, whose members usually disperse much earlier. The position close to the north celestial pole also makes it observable almost all year round from northern latitudes.

caldwell-C2.short_description: C2 (NGC 40), Planetary nebula in the constellation Cepheus. Small dimensions and relatively high contrast make it suitable for moderate magnification; atmospheric stability remains decisive for fine details. Its apparent scale is 0.6′; the integrated magnitude 11.6 does not alone describe what will be evident at the eyepiece.
caldwell-C2.observing_notes: On C2 (NGC 40), integrated magnitude 11.6, protect dark adaptation and evaluate edge, center and overlapping stars separately.
caldwell-C2.curiosity_text: The central star of NGC 40 is a very hot Wolf-Rayet that ejects material at great speed. The recent wind impacts previously lost slower layers and shapes the nebula's irregular shell.
